description: A composite figure made of a 12-row property table (top) plus twelve SEM fracture-surface micrographs labelled (a)–(l) below, each carrying a 10 µm scale bar. The table has the headers Nominal composition (at.%), Hardness of matrix (HB), Yield stress in compression (MPa), Yield stress in tension (MPa), Total elongation (%), and Mode of fracture; entries include Fe–15Al (159 HB, 356/344 MPa, 16% TGC), Fe–15Al–2Ti–1C (197, 485/420, 3.3%, TGC), Fe–15Al–2V–1C (191, 396/374, 0.6%, TGC), Fe–15Al–2Nb–1C (309, 827, –, –, TGC), Fe–15Al–2Ta–1C (291, 868, –, –, TGC), Fe–26Al (260, 644/475, 0.4%, TGC), Fe–26Al–2Ti–1C (251, 447/342, 0.7%, IGD+TGC), Fe–26Al–4Ti–1C (229, 454, –, –, IGD+TGC), Fe–26Al–2V–1C (286, 544/350, 0.5%, TGC), Fe–26Al–2Nb–1C (275, 601/427, 1.4%, TGC), Fe–26Al–4Nb–1C (303, 792, –, –, IGD+TGC) and Fe–26Al–2Ta–1C (288, 594, –, –, IGD+TGC). Micrographs (a)–(f) and (i),(j) show facetted transgranular cleavage; (g),(h) and (k),(l) additionally show smooth intergranular decohesion areas with cube-like or densely distributed precipitates. The figure links measured tensile ductility and fracture mode to the observed failure morphology of each alloy.

subfigures.description: Property table for 12 alloys listing nominal composition (at.%), Hardness of matrix (HB), Yield stress in compression (MPa), Yield stress in tension (MPa), Total elongation (%), and Mode of fracture. Values range from 159 to 309 HB for matrix hardness and 356 to 868 MPa for compression yield stress.
SEM fractograph of Fe–15Al, 10 µm scale bar, showing fine transgranular cleavage facets with river patterns; the alloy has 16% total elongation.
SEM fractograph of Fe–15Al–2Ti–1C, 10 µm scale bar, coarse transgranular cleavage facets and a large smooth cleavage plane.
SEM fractograph of Fe–15Al–2V–1C, 10 µm scale bar, coarse blocky transgranular cleavage with a smooth step-like facet.
SEM fractograph of Fe–15Al–2Nb–1C, 10 µm scale bar, coarse transgranular cleavage facets with elongated plates.
SEM fractograph of Fe–15Al–2Ta–1C, 10 µm scale bar, coarse transgranular cleavage facets.
SEM fractograph of Fe–26Al, 10 µm scale bar, very coarse transgranular fracture with a large smooth facet crossing the field.
SEM fractograph of Fe–26Al–2Ti–1C, 10 µm scale bar, mixed smooth intergranular areas bearing cube-like precipitates adjacent to facetted cleavage regions.
SEM fractograph of Fe–26Al–4Ti–1C, 10 µm scale bar, almost entirely smooth intergranular decohesion surface with scattered cube-like precipitates.
SEM fractograph of Fe–26Al–2V–1C, 10 µm scale bar, uniform step-like transgranular fracture with plate-like (needle-shaped) precipitates.
SEM fractograph of Fe–26Al–2Nb–1C, 10 µm scale bar, very fine facetted transgranular cleavage; this alloy has the highest ductility (1.4%) of the Fe–26Al-based alloys.
SEM fractograph of Fe–26Al–4Nb–1C, 10 µm scale bar, rough intergranular decohesion surface with densely distributed precipitates that disrupt the grain-boundary facets.
SEM fractograph of Fe–26Al–2Ta–1C, 10 µm scale bar, partially intergranular (smooth) and partially transgranular (facetted) fracture.

observations.observation: The table reports fracture mode TGC (transgranular cleavage) for all Fe–15Al-based alloys and for Fe–26Al, Fe–26Al–2V–1C and Fe–26Al–2Nb–1C, and IGD+TGC (intergranular decohesion plus transgranular cleavage) for Fe–26Al–2Ti–1C, Fe–26Al–4Ti–1C, Fe–26Al–4Nb–1C and Fe–26Al–2Ta–1C.

The table lists Total elongation (%) of 16 for Fe–15Al, the highest value in the table, falling to 3.3 (Fe–15Al–2Ti–1C), 0.6 (Fe–15Al–2V–1C), 0.4 (Fe–26Al), 0.7 (Fe–26Al–2Ti–1C), 0.5 (Fe–26Al–2V–1C) and 1.4 (Fe–26Al–2Nb–1C); all other alloys have a dash (–) in the tensile columns.

The table lists the highest yield stress in compression for Fe–15Al–2Ta–1C (868 MPa) and Fe–15Al–2Nb–1C (827 MPa), and the lowest matrix hardness of 159 HB for Fe–15Al versus a maximum of 309 HB for Fe–15Al–2Nb–1C.
Every fractograph (a)–(l) displays a 10 µm scale-bar marker in its lower-left corner and is a secondary-electron SEM image of a tensile fracture surface.
Panel (g) and (h) (Fe–26Al–2Ti–1C and Fe–26Al–4Ti–1C) show smooth intergranular areas carrying cube-like precipitates.
Panel (k) (Fe–26Al–4Nb–1C) shows an intergranular decohesion surface that is rough rather than smooth because of densely distributed precipitates.

The caption states the fractographs are of the investigated alloys after tensile testing at room temperature, with (a) Fe–15Al; (b)–(e) Fe–15Al–2M–1C for M = Ti, V, Nb, Ta; (f) Fe–26Al; (g),(i),(j),(l) Fe–26Al–2M–1C for M = Ti, V, Nb, Ta; and (h),(k) Fe–26Al–4M–1C for M = Ti, Nb.

The binary Fe–15Al alloy, with ductility of 16%, fractured by transgranular fracture with very fine cleavage facets (Fig. 4a), while all Fe–15Al–2M–1C alloys fractured with coarse transgranular cleavage (Fig. 4b–e).

Fe–15Al–2Ti–1C has the highest room-temperature ductility (~3.3%) of all Fe–15Al-based alloys, and Fe–26Al–2Nb–1C the highest (~1.4%) of all Fe–26Al-based alloys, the latter exhibiting very fine facetted transgranular cleavage (Fig. 4j).
The fracture facets of Fe–26Al–2V–1C are stated to form on the (001) planes of the matrix parallel to the (001) planes of the plate-like vanadium carbide precipitates, based on a previous study [21].
Fe–26Al–4Ti–1C fractured almost completely by intergranular decohesion, and Fe–26Al–4Ti–1C together with Fe–26Al–4Nb–1C show totally brittle behaviour at room temperature.
